title: Using Tailwind tokens to keep a portfolio consistent
description: How semantic colors, spacing, gradients, and reusable component classes keep a custom interface coherent.
hero: Tailwind is most effective when it becomes a design system API. The goal is not to memorize utilities, but to create a small vocabulary that keeps the interface coherent.

sections.heading: Use semantic color names
body: Raw colors like cyan or slate are useful, but semantic colors communicate intent. Tokens such as ink, surface, accent, success, and warning make components easier to reason about.
They also make theme switching much easier because the component asks for a role, not a specific color.

sections.heading: Create reusable component classes sparingly
body: A class like glass-panel is useful because it bundles repeated visual decisions: border, background, blur, radius, and shadow. A class that hides one utility is usually not worth it.
The best abstractions remove repeated judgment while keeping the markup understandable.

sections.heading: Keep motion tokenized too
body: Animation names such as reveal, float, and marquee make motion decisions reusable. They also make it easier to adjust timing globally instead of tuning every component by hand.
Motion belongs in the visual system, not only in individual components.

takeaways: Treat motion as part of the design system.
